phonemes.desc: M followed by open [a]; the root marz- belongs to the cold family of marznąć, 'to freeze'.
Voiced [z] plus [a]; this syllable carries the stress, the name's single pitch peak.
The geminate double n is held a full beat — the frozen pause of a winter name.

pronunciation.approximation: mar-ZAH-nah — the stress falls on the second syllable, and the double n is held longer than English allows.

kin.label: Polish
kin.form: marzanna — from marz-, 'frost' (marznąć, 'to freeze, to grow numb'), or else connected to mora, 'nightmare, female death-spirit'

kin.label: West Slavic
kin.form: Morana / Morena (Czech, Slovak, Sorbian) — the same winter-death goddess under her 'death' name

kin.label: PIE (hypothesis)
kin.form: *mer-, 'to die, to decay' — Latin mors/mortis, Greek móros; scholars divide between the frost and the death etymology

pronunciation.note: Marzanna is Tier 2: the Polish name is plain ASCII, and no diacritic or distinctive letter distinguishes the restoration from the domain form. What the capitalized restoration restores is not orthography but standing — the scholarly citation of a living Slavic goddess.

domains.title: Marzanna
domains.subtitle: Winter
domains.lead: Marzanna is the Slavic goddess of winter, frost, and death — the withering power whose departure is celebrated each spring. Her name belongs to the cold family of Polish marznąć, 'to freeze,' and her kinship with the nightmare-hag mora ties her to the dying of the year itself. Every March her effigy is drowned so the world can thaw.

cards.name: Winter's Rule
cards.desc: From autumn to early spring she governs the frozen months: fields locked in frost, rivers stilled, the sun weak and low.

cards.name: Death and the Dying Year
cards.desc: Her domain includes the death of the old year — the withered hag whose reign must end before anything can grow.

cards.name: The Drowning Rite
cards.desc: Each spring, in Zielone Świątki ('Green Week'), her straw effigy is carried out and drowned — driving winter from the village.

cards.name: The Morana Family
cards.desc: Under the names Morana, Morena, and Mara she is honored across Poland, the Czech lands, Slovakia, and the Balkans.

symbols.name: The straw effigy
symbols.meaning: The braided doll of rags and straw drowned in the river — the goddess made portable, so the village itself could carry her out.

symbols.name: The river
symbols.meaning: The running water that receives her each spring; drowning is not execution but return.

symbols.name: Green boughs (gaik)
symbols.meaning: The green branches brought back from the drowning — proof that life returns the moment she leaves.

symbols.name: Frost
symbols.meaning: Her visible body on window glass and ploughed earth — the signature she leaves on the world.

symbols.name: The last ice
symbols.meaning: The final snowdrift at the village edge, where the effigy is sometimes burned instead of drowned — the season's funeral pyre.

mythology.lead: Marzanna is a goddess of ritual, not text: no Slavic epic survives to tell her story, so her mythology lives in the calendar — in the spring drownings, the dirges for drowned maidens, and the folk etymologies that name her Frost or Nightmare. The sources are ethnographic and late; the feeling they preserve is very old.

myths.title: Death to the Winter Queen
myths.text: Every spring, in the week the church calendar calls Zielone Świątki ('Green Week'), villages across Poland carry Marzanna out of the settlement: a doll of straw and rags dressed as a woman, crowned, shawled, and splashed with water as she goes. The procession winds to the river or the last snowdrift, where the effigy is beaten, burned, or — most often — thrown into the current and held under until she drowns. The children sing that Marzanna is dead, and they carry home green boughs, the gaik, to prove that life has returned with her going. Jan Máchal described the rite for the Mythology of All Races survey in 1918, and Polish ethnography has recorded it without a break into the twenty-first century. The myth built into the ritual is stark and unsentimental: winter is a goddess, and the year cannot turn until she is dead. The village does not mourn her. It drowns her.

myths.title: The Lament for Kostroma
myths.text: North of Poland the mourning falls on a different name. In the cycle assembled by A. N. Afanasyev and printed by Máchal (Slavic Mythology, 1918), Russian girls sing spring dirges for Kostroma, a maiden of the rites. In one legend she is the daughter of the Polotsk prince Samo; walking on the Volga's bank she fell asleep, the water-nymphs came and braided her hair, played with her — and drowned her. Her death was mourned like a calamity, with funeral songs, and the mourning ended by burying a straw effigy in her place. Afanasyev argued that the dirges preserve a dying vegetation goddess behind the maiden, a reading later scholars have accepted with caution: the songs are genuine folklore, the goddess is inference. Whether Kostroma is Marzanna under another name is exactly the kind of question the fragmentary Slavic record cannot settle. The grief, at least, is real — and it is the grief due to the dying of the year.

myths.title: Marzanna and Jarilo
myths.text: The fullest modern telling pairs her with a young god. In the reconstruction of Boris Rybakov (Ancient Slavic Paganism, 1981), Marzanna belongs to a seasonal drama: Jarilo (Jarovit), the youthful power of spring vegetation and erotic force, dies each year, and winter — Marzanna — reigns over his absence until the rites call him back. Rybakov read the cycle out of calendar customs, wedding songs, and comparative Indo-European parallels. It must be said plainly: no medieval Slavic text narrates this story. It is a modern construction from folklore, and specialists dispute its details. Yet the pattern it assembles — a dying young god, a reigning hag of frost, a spring release sealed by water — matches rites that were genuinely performed for centuries, and it gives Marzanna a narrative worthy of the dread her name carries.

myths.title: Frost or Death-Spirit?
myths.text: Her name is itself the myth's riddle, and linguists still divide over it. One school derives Marzanna from Polish marz-, 'frost' (marznąć, 'to freeze, to grow numb') — the goddess as the frozen months given a body. Another connects her to the Slavic mora, the female night-hag who crouches on sleepers' chests, a word that survives in English 'nightmare'; on this reading she is less a season than a death-spirit who owns the season. Both derivations run into the cold and the dead, and her cousins across the Slavic world carry the second name openly: Morana in the Czech lands, Morena in Slovakia, Mara in the Balkans. Medieval church synods raged against her rites for centuries. A goddess whose own name resists etymology is a goddess who holds both meanings at once: winter as frost, and winter as the little death that must be drowned each spring.

lore.syncretism: Christianity did not erase Marzanna; it rescheduled her. The drowning migrated to Zielone Świątki, the 'Green Week' after Pentecost, so that a pagan death-rite could wear the church's calendar, and medieval Polish synodal statutes thunder against the custom for centuries — the surest proof it never died. Her identity also split along her etymologies: where the frost reading dominated she remained a personified winter; where the mora reading survived she shaded into the night-hag, the rusalka's colder cousin, and into the whole Slavic company of female spirits of death and water. Modernity returned her to dignity: the drowning of Marzanna entered Poland's national register of intangible cultural heritage in the twenty-first century, and Slavic neopaganism (Rodnovery) now worships her openly as a goddess of winter, death, and the rebirth that only her departure makes possible.
lore.culturalLegacy: The drowning of Marzanna is not folklore embalmed in a book; it is a living custom. Every March, Polish schoolchildren still braid her effigy, march it to the river, and throw it in — television covers it, ethnologists measure it, and the rite stands on the Polish national register of intangible cultural heritage. Her wider family stays busy: Morana is drowned in the Czech lands and Slovakia each spring, and Rusalka week in early summer belongs to the same watery calendar of female spirits. In language she survives on both sides of her disputed etymology — in 'nightmare,' if the mora school is right, and in the very word for freezing, if the frost school is. And in the new Slavic paganism she has come fully back: not a demon to be exorcised each spring, but a goddess to be addressed — winter, death, and return, honored in her own right.
lore.extendedMeditation: Most cultures personify the good seasons; the Slavs dared to personify the bad one. Marzanna is the honest goddess: winter without apology, old age and frost and the failure of things, given a woman's face and a woman's name. What her rite teaches is bracing. You do not appease winter, and you do not wait it out in reverent silence; you make a doll of it, carry it to the river in procession, singing, and hold it under. Renewal is not a mood but an act — an act with a body count of one, gladly paid. There is also a darker reading available. The effigy is a woman, and the village drowns her so the crops can grow. However we judge that image, the ritual holds it up every spring and lets us look. Perhaps that is the deepest use of Marzanna: a culture keeping, in public and with its children watching, a ceremony that admits winter must be killed — and asks who, each year, does the killing.

lore.archaeology: Marzanna left no temples, statues, or inscriptions — the early Slavs built in wood and wrote little — so her material record is the rite itself. Ethnographic museums in Warsaw and Kraków hold collections of the drowned effigies, rescued from rivers by curators: straw women in shawls, each one a winter actually ended. The written evidence is mostly hostile: medieval Polish church synods repeatedly condemned the drowning and the songs that went with it, which lets us track the custom backward through the condemnations for centuries. Archaeology adds only indirect light — early-medieval Slavic river cult sites with votive deposits are known — but the rite's continuity needs no dig: it has eyewitnesses, from 16th-century clergy complaining about it to news crews filming it this March.
